title: My children have won (Bava Metzia 59b)
hookLine: Elijah reports God smiling: my children have defeated me

cards: A parent and a kid, playing chess. For years the parent wins every game, gently. Then one day the kid sees a move the parent missed, and wins, fair and square.
Watch the parent's face: a little shock, and then a grin that won't go away. Yesterday the sages told a voice from heaven, it is not in heaven, and overruled it. You might expect thunder.
The Talmud tells what God did instead.

teach.h: WHAT DID GOD DO IN THAT HOUR?
teach.b: Right after the argument over the oven, the Talmud tells a short scene. Rabbi Natan once meets the prophet Elijah, who in Jewish tradition wanders the earth and shows up at key moments.
Rabbi Natan asks: what did the Holy One do in that hour, when the sages refused the heavenly voice?
Elijah says: he smiled, and said, my children have defeated me, my children have defeated me.

In the story, God isn't angry at being overruled, but delighted, like a parent whose children have grown up enough to reason for themselves. The teaching was given so they would take it and think with it, and they did.
But the Talmud doesn't stop with the smile. The same page tells what happened next on earth. Rabbi Eliezer, who had been outvoted, was put under a ban.
The things he had ruled pure were burned. Rabbi Akiva, his student, dressed in black to bring him the news gently, and sat at a distance, weeping.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO LOST WAS HURT.
teach.b: And the Talmud says great harm followed, because Rabbi Eliezer had been so deeply hurt. That may be part of why this story sits in a chapter about wounding people with words.
Winning an argument is one thing. How you treat the person who lost is another. The Talmud holds both: God's joy at the argument, and grief at the wound.

how: Jewish study is often done in pairs or groups who argue over the text, and being shown a better reading by a partner is considered part of learning, not a defeat.

s: the Talmud says God was angry at being overruled
Elijah says God smiled: my children have defeated me.
the story ends happily for everyone
Rabbi Eliezer was banned and deeply hurt, and the Talmud mourns it.
this story sits in a chapter about hurting people with words
the page moves from the argument to the wound.

games.q: you've just won a big argument, fair and square. the person who lost is your teacher, and he's hurt. what do you do?
o: bring the news gently, and sit with him.
games.why: Rabbi Akiva dressed in black, went to Rabbi Eliezer, and told him gently, sitting at a distance, in tears.

practice: Remember a time someone out-argued you and they were right: how did it feel, and where in your body? Picture meeting that moment with a grin instead, the way the parent grins at the chessboard: good move.
Then remember an argument you won, and if the other person was hurt, picture going back to them, gently.
